items.topic: IV potassium — never administer as IV push/bolus; use diluted infusion
items.stem: A provider orders IV potassium chloride for a hospitalized client with hypokalemia. Which nursing action is essential for safe administration?

options.text: Never give potassium as an IV push or bolus; administer only as a diluted IV infusion at a controlled rate
Push undiluted potassium chloride concentrate rapidly through a peripheral IV for fastest correction
Add concentrated potassium to a running IV and bolus the line without an infusion pump
Give the entire daily potassium deficit as a single undiluted IV push at the start of the shift

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Pharmacology: never push or bolus potassium IV—rapid administration can cause dysrhythmias and death; use premixed/diluted infusions. Merck: when IV potassium is required, give as infusion with concentration and rate limits (e.g., routine ≤10 mEq/hour; peripheral concentration ≤40 mEq/L).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Undiluted IV push of potassium concentrate can be fatal.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rapid uncontrolled bolus bypasses safe infusion controls.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Deficits are replaced with controlled infusion, not a single undiluted push.

sources.title: 5.2 Electrolytes
sources.section: Safety Alert — Potassium and IV Bolus or Push
sources.evidence: Never push or bolus potassium intravenously; rapid IV bolus/push can cause cardiac dysrhythmias and death; solutions are often premixed/diluted.

sources.title: Hypokalemia

items.topic: NGN cloze — IV potassium never push; diluted controlled infusion
items.stem: Complete the safety teaching for intravenous potassium chloride replacement.

ngn.template: Nurses must never give potassium as an IV {B1}; instead, administer a {B2} infusion, commonly keeping routine peripheral rates within limits such as about {B3}.

rationales.B1a: Correct. Never give potassium as an IV push or bolus (OpenStax).
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Piggyback on a pump is an infusion method, not the forbidden action named here.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Diluted infusion is the correct route modality, not the forbidden action.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Oral liquid may be used when appropriate but does not answer the IV safety blank.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Administer diluted, rate-controlled IV infusion (OpenStax/Merck).
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Undiluted concentrate IV push/bolus is dangerous.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Free-flow gravity bolus lacks safe rate control.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Potassium replacement is not given as an IM depot for this indication.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Merck: routine infusion rates should not exceed about 10 mEq/hour with concentration limits.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. 100 mEq in 1 minute is a lethal rapid bolus pattern.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Client preference does not override safe infusion limits.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Undiluted push dosing is contraindicated.

items.topic: Subcutaneous heparin — abdomen ≥2 inches from umbilicus; do not massage
items.stem: The nurse prepares to give subcutaneous unfractionated heparin. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Inject into the abdomen at least 2 inches (5 cm) from the umbilicus and do not massage the site afterward
Inject into the deltoid IM and vigorously massage to speed absorption
Always inject directly into the umbilicus and rub hard for 2 minutes
Give as an IV push of undiluted concentrate through a central line without verification

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Clinical Skills: preferred heparin SQ site is abdomen ≥2 in from umbilicus; do not massage (hematoma risk). Open RN Skills: abdomen >2 inches from umbilicus; do not massage after heparin.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Heparin prophylaxis is subcutaneous, not IM deltoid with massage.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Avoid the umbilicus; massage increases hematoma risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. This item addresses subcutaneous technique, not unverified IV concentrate push.

items.topic: NGN matrix — subcutaneous heparin administration actions indicated vs not
items.stem: For subcutaneous heparin administration, indicate whether each nurse action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Select an abdominal site at least about 2 inches away from the umbilicus and rotate sites
After injection, avoid massaging the site (gentle pressure with gauze is acceptable)
Vigorously massage the abdomen for several minutes to ‘work the heparin in’
Inject into visibly bruised, hard, or tender tissue to ‘use up’ that area first
Give the dose intramuscularly into the deltoid and rub hard afterward

rationales.R2: Indicated. Do not massage after heparin; gentle pressure OK (Open RN/OpenStax).
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Massage increases hematoma risk.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Subcutaneous technique, not IM with massage.

items.topic: Infant feeding safety — no honey under 12 months (infant botulism risk)
items.jurisdiction_note: Health Canada infant botulism guidance (honey linked in Canada); CDC concordant
items.stem: Parents ask whether they can put a little honey on their 6-month-old’s soother. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Do not give any honey (including on food, formula, water, or soothers) until the infant is over 1 year old because of infant botulism risk
Honey is required daily for all infants starting at 2 months to prevent constipation
Any heated honey is always sterile and safe for newborns
Only raw honey is unsafe; pasteurized honey is risk-free for infants

rationales.A: Correct. Health Canada: do not give any honey to infants <1 year; never add to food/water/formula/soother. CDC: no honey before 12 months; do not add to food, water, formula, or pacifier.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Honey is not a required infant remedy and is contraindicated under age 1.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Spores are not easily destroyed by heat/cooking.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Health Canada notes spores may be in pasteurized and unpasteurized honey.

items.topic: Breastfeeding latch — wide mouth, deep latch with chin into breast and flanged lips
items.stem: A postpartum client reports nipple pain with feeding. Which teaching best promotes an effective deep latch?

options.text: Wait for a wide-open mouth, bring the baby to the breast so the chin presses into the breast, and aim for a deep latch with flanged lips
Only place the tip of the nipple between tightly pursed lips and keep the baby’s chin away from the breast
Force the latch while the mouth is barely open and pull the breast to the baby across the crib
Avoid any areola in the mouth and stop feeding at the first swallow

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: wait for wide mouth; bring baby to breast; nipple deep; chin deep into breast; lips flanged. OWH: chin to breast, wide mouth, deep latch signs include comfort and flanged lips.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Shallow nipple-only latch causes pain and poor transfer.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Forcing a barely open mouth is ineffective and traumatic.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Effective latch includes more breast/areola tissue, not nipple tip only.

sources.title: 24.1 Basic Newborn Care
sources.evidence: Wide-open mouth; baby to breast; nipple deep; more areola below; lips flanged; chin deep into breast.

items.topic: Therapeutic communication — clarifying ambiguous client statements
items.stem: A client says, “Everything is useless now.” Which nurse response best uses clarification?

options.text: “I’m not sure I understand what you mean by useless—can you give an example of what feels useless?”
“Don’t say that—you should feel grateful you are here.”
“Let’s talk about the cafeteria menu instead.”
“Everyone feels useless sometimes, so it doesn’t matter.”

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: clarifying helps when communication is confusing/ambiguous. Open RN: clarification asks the client to further define meaning (example: “I’m not sure I understand… can you give an example?”).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Changing the subject is a barrier.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Minimizing dismisses the client’s experience.

items.topic: Pediatric oral health — pea-sized fluoride toothpaste for ages 3–6; supervise and spit
items.stem: A parent asks how much fluoride toothpaste to use for a 4-year-old. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Use a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste, supervise brushing, and teach the child to spit rather than swallow
Fill the entire brush head with adult toothpaste and have the child swallow it for systemic benefit
Never use fluoride toothpaste at any age because fluorosis is inevitable with pea-sized amounts
Use a full ribbon of toothpaste and rinse vigorously with mouthwash after every brush

rationales.A: Correct. CPS Caring for Kids: by age 3–4 use pea-sized fluoride toothpaste; spit; supervise. CDC: ages 3–6 use no more than pea-sized amount; teach spit, not swallow.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Excess toothpaste increases swallowing/fluorosis risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Age-appropriate fluoride toothpaste prevents decay when used correctly.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Full ribbon exceeds pediatric amount guidance.

items.jurisdiction_note: Ontario O. Reg. 799/93 professional misconduct + CNO Documentation standard
items.topic: Ontario — falsifying a practice record is professional misconduct
items.stem: An Ontario nurse is asked by a colleague to backdate a medication administration entry that was never given. Which response reflects professional accountability?

options.text: Refuse—falsifying a record relating to nursing practice is professional misconduct and documentation must remain accurate
Agree to falsify the entry if it helps the unit’s chart audit scores
Delete another nurse’s notes so the timeline looks cleaner
Document the medication as given before it is administered to save time

rationales.A: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 lists falsifying a record relating to the member’s practice as professional misconduct. CNO Documentation: nurses must not falsify a record, including signing/issuing documents known to be false or misleading.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Falsification remains misconduct regardless of workplace pressure.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Altering/deleting others’ documentation is prohibited.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO: do not document before care is provided.

sources.title: O. Reg. 799/93: PROFESSIONAL MISCONDUCT
sources.evidence: Acts of professional misconduct include failing to keep records as required and falsifying a record relating to the member’s practice.

sources.title: Documentation
sources.evidence: Do not falsify a record; do not document before care; do not delete/alter others’ documentation.

items.jurisdiction_note: Ontario O. Reg. 799/93 professional misconduct + CNO Documentation standard
items.topic: NGN cloze — Ontario record-keeping and falsification misconduct
items.stem: Complete the statement about Ontario nursing documentation and professional misconduct.

ngn.template: Under O. Reg. 799/93, {B1} and {B2} are acts of professional misconduct; CNO also requires nurses to document in a {B3} manner and never document before care is provided.

B1.text: failing to keep records as required

B2.text: falsifying a record relating to the member’s practice

rationales.B1a: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 lists failing to keep records as required as professional misconduct.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is essential care but not the records misconduct clause.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. SBAR is communication technique, not the misconduct element named here.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Name badges are identification practice, not the record-keeping clause.
rationales.B2a: Correct. O. Reg. 799/93 lists falsifying a record relating to the member’s practice as misconduct.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Clarifying questions are therapeutic communication, not falsification.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Therapeutic silence is not a misconduct element.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Offering self is a therapeutic technique, not falsification.
rationales.B3a: Correct. CNO Documentation requires clear, complete, accurate, timely documentation.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Vague/optional documentation fails the standard.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Pre-charting before care is prohibited.
